title: The Invention of the Printing Press
summary: How Johannes Gutenberg invented the printing press, using movable metal type to make books far faster and cheaper than copying them by hand.
poll: The invention of the printing press changed how people share ideas more than almost any other invention in history.

versions.title: The Invention of the Printing Press
versions.text:
Long ago, books were made by hand. This took a long time. One book took months. Books cost a lot.

A man named Gutenberg had an idea. He wanted to print books fast. He used metal letters. He tried many tests.

He was not alone. Other lands had tried print too. But he made a new press.

He made small metal letters. He could move the letters. He pressed them on paper. Ink made words show up.

He printed a big book. It was a Bible. Many copies came out fast.

Today, books are everywhere. We can read many books. We thank him for this gift.

versions.title: The Invention of the Printing Press
versions.text:
Long before printing existed, every book had to be copied entirely by hand, and these copies were never fast, since monks and writers copied each page one at a time, which took a very long time. One book could take many months to finish, and books were extremely costly as a result, so only wealthy people could usually afford one.

A man named Johannes Gutenberg had a bold idea, so he set out to find a way to print books much faster than before. He worked with small metal letters inside his own busy workshop. He tried test after test without ever giving up, night after long night.

Gutenberg was not the first person with this idea, since other lands had experimented with printing long before him. Both China and Korea had early forms of movable type. But Gutenberg's new press, which combined metal letters with ink and a sturdy press, worked far better than anything that had come before it in Europe.

He made tiny metal letters that could be reused again and again to spell many different words, and he arranged these letters carefully to form whole pages of text. Then he pressed them firmly onto paper using ink, over and over again.

Gutenberg printed a huge book known as a Bible, and remarkably, many copies came out much faster than anyone had ever managed before. This single, remarkable achievement changed how books were produced forever, across the whole of Europe.

Today, books are everywhere we look, and we can read as many books as we want without any trouble at all, almost anywhere we go. We can thank Gutenberg for starting this amazing change in how people share ideas.

versions.title: The Invention of the Printing Press
versions.text:
Long before printing existed, every book had to be copied entirely by hand, and these copies were never fast, since monks and scribes copied each page one at a time in a cramped workshop, which took a very long time. One book could take many months to finish, and books were extremely costly as a result, so very few people could ever afford one.

A man named Johannes Gutenberg had a bold idea, so he set out to invent a way to print books much faster than before. He worked with small metal letters inside his own busy workshop, assisted by several skilled helpers, trying test after test without ever giving up, night after exhausting night.

Gutenberg was certainly not the first person with this idea, since other lands had experimented with printing long before him, and both China and Korea had early forms of movable type. But Gutenberg's new press, which combined metal type, ink, and a sturdy mechanism, worked far better than anything that had come before it in Europe.

He made tiny metal letters that could be reused again and again to spell many different words, and he arranged these letters carefully to form whole pages of text. Then he pressed them firmly onto paper using ink, over and over again, page after page.

Gutenberg's invention became known as the printing press, and remarkably, many copies of a book could now be produced far faster than ever before. This single discovery transformed how books were produced forever across the whole of Europe, and eventually the entire world.

Today, printed books are everywhere we look, and we can read as many books as we want without any trouble at all. We can thank Gutenberg for starting this enormous change in how people share and preserve ideas.

versions.title: The Invention of the Printing Press

A man named Johannes Gutenberg was determined to invent a way to print books much faster than before, so he worked with small metal letters inside his own busy workshop, assisted by several skilled helpers. Together they tried experiment after experiment without ever giving up, night after exhausting night.

Gutenberg was certainly not the first person with this idea. Other lands had experimented with printing long before him, and both China and Korea had developed early forms of movable type many centuries earlier than Gutenberg's own effort. But Gutenberg's new press, which combined metal type, ink, and a sturdy mechanism, worked far better than anything that had come before it in Europe.

He manufactured tiny metal letters that could be reused repeatedly to spell many different words. He arranged these letters carefully to form entire pages of readable text. Then he pressed them firmly onto paper using ink, over and over again, page after careful page, until every copy matched.

Gutenberg's invention became known as the printing press, and remarkably, many copies of a single book could now be produced far faster than ever before. This singular discovery permanently transformed how books were produced across the whole of Europe, and it eventually changed the entire world.

Today, printed books are everywhere we look, and we can read as many books as we want without any real difficulty at all, in any language we choose. We can thank Gutenberg for starting this enormous and lasting change in how people share and preserve their ideas.

versions.title: The Invention of the Printing Press
versions.text:
Before printing existed, every book had to be copied entirely by hand. These copies were never especially swift, since monks and scribes copied each page individually inside a cramped workshop, which required a truly considerable amount of time and effort. One book could require many months to finish, and books were extremely costly as a result, so very few ordinary people could ever realistically afford to own even a single copy of their very own.

A man named Johannes Gutenberg was determined to invent a method for printing books much faster than before, so he worked with small metal letters inside his own busy workshop, assisted by several genuinely skilled helpers. Together they attempted experiment after experiment without ever abandoning the demanding project, night after exhausting night, for several difficult, uncertain years.

Gutenberg was certainly not the first person to pursue this idea. Other regions had experimented with printing long before him, and both China and Korea had developed early forms of movable type many centuries earlier than Gutenberg's own careful and determined effort in Europe. But Gutenberg's innovative press, which combined metal type, specially mixed ink, and a sturdy mechanism, functioned far more reliably than anything that had come before it anywhere in Europe. Few people had ever imagined such remarkable speed was truly achievable.

He meticulously manufactured tiny metal letters that could be reused repeatedly to spell countless different words. He arranged these letters meticulously and patiently to form entire pages of readable text, then pressed them firmly onto paper using ink, repeatedly, page after careful page, until each copy matched precisely.

Gutenberg's groundbreaking invention eventually became known throughout Europe as the printing press. Remarkably, many identical copies of a single book could now be produced far more rapidly and reliably than ever before. This singular discovery permanently transformed how books were produced across the whole of Europe, and it eventually transformed the entire world beyond anyone's expectations.

Today, printed books are everywhere we look, and we can read as many books as we truly desire without any real difficulty whatsoever, in almost any language we might choose to read. We can thank Gutenberg for initiating this enormous and lasting transformation in how people everywhere create, share, and preserve their own ideas.

versions.title: The Invention of the Printing Press
versions.text:
Before the advent of printing, every book had to be laboriously copied entirely by hand. These copies were never especially swift, since monks and scribes painstakingly copied each individual page inside a cramped workshop, which required a truly considerable investment of time and effort. One book could require many months to finish, and books were extraordinarily costly as a result, so very few ordinary people could ever realistically afford to own even a single copy of their very own, however badly they might want one.

A man named Johannes Gutenberg was fiercely and relentlessly determined to invent a method for printing books considerably faster than before, so he labored with small metal letters inside his own busy workshop, assisted by several genuinely skilled helpers. Together they attempted experiment after experiment without ever abandoning the demanding project, night after exhausting night, across several long, difficult, and uncertain years.

Gutenberg was certainly not the first person to pursue this idea. Other regions had experimented extensively with printing long before him, and both China and Korea had independently developed early forms of movable type many centuries earlier than Gutenberg's own meticulous and determined effort in distant Europe. But Gutenberg's innovative press, which ingeniously combined metal type, specially formulated ink, and a sturdy mechanical frame, functioned far more reliably than anything that had previously existed anywhere in Europe. Few people had ever imagined such remarkable speed was truly achievable.

He meticulously manufactured tiny metal letters that could be reused repeatedly to spell countless different words. He arranged these letters meticulously and patiently to form entire pages of readable text, then pressed them firmly onto paper using ink, repeatedly, page after careful page, until each finished copy matched the others precisely.

Gutenberg's groundbreaking invention eventually became known throughout Europe as the printing press. Remarkably, many identical copies of a single book could now be produced far more rapidly and reliably than ever before. This singular discovery permanently and irrevocably transformed how books were produced across the whole of Europe, and it eventually transformed the entire world beyond anyone's wildest expectations.

Today, printed books are everywhere we look, and we can read as many books as we truly desire without any real difficulty whatsoever, in almost any language we personally might choose to read. We can thank Gutenberg for initiating this enormous and lasting transformation in how people everywhere create, share, and preserve their own ideas.

versions.title: The Invention of the Printing Press
versions.text:
Before the advent of printing, every book had to be laboriously copied entirely by hand. These copies were never especially swift, since monks and scribes painstakingly copied each individual page inside a cramped, dimly lit workshop, which required a truly considerable investment of time, patience, and effort. One book could require many months or even years to finish, and books were extraordinarily and prohibitively costly as a result, so very few ordinary people could ever realistically afford to own even a single copy of their very own.

A man named Johannes Gutenberg was fiercely and relentlessly determined to invent a method for printing books considerably faster than before, so he labored tirelessly with small metal letters inside his own busy workshop, assisted by several genuinely skilled and dedicated helpers. Together they attempted experiment after exhausting experiment without ever abandoning the demanding, ambitious project, night after sleepless night, across several long, difficult, and uncertain years.

Gutenberg was certainly not the first person to pursue this particular idea. Other regions had experimented extensively with printing long before him, and both China and Korea had independently developed early forms of movable type many centuries earlier than Gutenberg's own meticulous and determined effort in distant Europe. But Gutenberg's innovative press, which ingeniously combined metal type, specially formulated ink, and a sturdy mechanical frame, functioned far more reliably and efficiently than anything that had previously existed anywhere in Europe. Few people had ever truly imagined such remarkable speed was genuinely achievable at all.

He meticulously manufactured countless tiny metal letters that could be reused repeatedly to spell virtually any different words imaginable. He arranged these letters meticulously and patiently to form entire pages of readable, legible text, then pressed them firmly onto paper using specially prepared ink, repeatedly, page after painstaking page, until each finished copy matched the others with remarkable precision.

Gutenberg's groundbreaking invention eventually became renowned throughout Europe as the printing press. Remarkably, many identical copies of a single book could now be produced far more rapidly, reliably, and affordably than ever before. This singular discovery permanently and irrevocably transformed how books were produced across the whole of Europe, and it eventually transformed the entire world beyond anyone's wildest expectations.

Today, printed books are ubiquitous wherever we look, and we can read as many books as we truly desire without any real difficulty whatsoever, in almost any language we personally might choose to read. We can thank Gutenberg for initiating this truly enormous and lasting transformation in how human beings everywhere create, share, and preserve their own ideas forever.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How monks lived and prayed inside their quiet workshops in Europe
How Gutenberg invented a press that could print books quickly
Why the Bible is an important book to read
How paper is made from trees today
questions.why: The article explains how Gutenberg built a printing press that let books be made much faster than copying them by hand.

wrong.A: Monk life is only briefly mentioned, not the article's main focus.
wrong.C: The Bible is used as an example, not the article's main topic.
wrong.D: How paper is made from trees is never discussed in the article.

questions.stem: How were books made before the printing press?
options: They were printed by machines inside large factories
They were written only by young children in schools
They were copied by hand, one page at a time
They were painted onto the walls of deep caves
questions.why: The article explains that before the press, books had to be copied by hand, one page at a time, which took a long time.

wrong.A: Machines and factories came only after the press was invented.
wrong.B: Children writing books in schools is never mentioned.
wrong.D: Cave paintings are never mentioned in the article.

questions.stem: What did Gutenberg use to print words onto paper?
options: Large flat stone tablets carved by hand
Colorful paint applied with soft brushes
Thin strips of woven cloth and thread
Small metal letters pressed with ink
questions.why: The article explains that Gutenberg used small metal letters, pressed with ink, to print words onto paper.

wrong.A: Stone tablets are not mentioned as part of Gutenberg's press.
wrong.B: Paint and brushes are not described as part of the invention.
wrong.C: Cloth strips are never mentioned in the article.

questions.stem: Why was it a problem that books took months to copy by hand?
options: Books became too expensive and rare for most people
Books became too heavy for most people to carry
Books became too colorful for young children to read
Books became too short and simple to be useful
questions.why: The article shows that because copying took so long, books cost a lot, so very few people could own them.

wrong.B: Weight is never discussed in connection with hand-copied books.
wrong.C: Color is never mentioned as a problem with books.
wrong.D: Length is never discussed as a problem with hand-copied books.

questions.stem: Why do you think Gutenberg's metal letters could be used again and again?
options: Because they were painted a slightly different color each time
Because they melted away after every single use
Because they could be moved and rearranged to spell new words
Because they were simply thrown away after just one book
questions.why: Since the letters could be moved around to spell different words, Gutenberg could reuse the same set of letters for many different pages and books.

wrong.A: Color is never mentioned as a feature of the metal letters.
wrong.B: The letters did not melt; they could be reused many times.
wrong.D: The letters were reused, not thrown away.

questions.stem: In the article, what does the word "fast" describe?
options: Something that takes a very long time to happen
Something that happens in a short amount of time
Something that is very heavy to carry
Something that is very expensive to buy
questions.why: In the article, "fast" describes printing happening quickly, unlike the slow process of copying books by hand.

wrong.A: Fast means quick, the opposite of taking a long time.
wrong.C: Fast describes speed, not weight.
wrong.D: Fast describes speed, not cost.

questions.stem: What happened after Gutenberg printed his big book?
options: Handwritten books became the only books anyone wanted
Many copies of books could be made much faster than before
People stopped reading books
Monks began copying books even more slowly
questions.why: After Gutenberg's printing press worked, the article explains that many copies of books could be produced much faster than before.

wrong.A: Printed books became more common, not handwritten ones.
wrong.C: The article shows people reading more books, not fewer.
wrong.D: Monks copying more slowly is never mentioned in the article.

questions.stem: How was printing in Gutenberg's time different from copying books by hand?
options: Printing made many copies fast, while hand copying made one slow copy at a time
Printing used no ink, while hand copying used lots of ink
Printing needed no letters, while hand copying needed many letters
Printing was done by children, while hand copying was done by monks in the old cities
questions.why: The article shows that printing could make many copies quickly, while copying by hand could only make one slow copy at a time.

wrong.B: Printing used ink too; that is how words appeared on the page.
wrong.C: Printing also used letters, just made of metal instead of handwriting.
wrong.D: The article does not say printing was done only by children.

LOW.prompt: Explain how Gutenberg's printing press changed the way books were made.
checklist: Did you mention how books were copied before the press?
Did you explain what the metal letters did?
Did you say why the press was better?
LOW.modelAnswer: Before the printing press, books were copied by hand, which took months and made books very expensive. Gutenberg had an idea to use small metal letters that could be moved around to spell new words. He pressed the letters onto paper with ink, and many copies came out fast. This let many more people finally get books of their own.

MID.prompt: Explain why Gutenberg's printing press was such an important breakthrough for how people got and shared books.
checklist: Did you explain why hand-copied books were so costly?
Did you mention Gutenberg's testing in his workshop?
Did you explain the lasting effect of his achievement?
MID.modelAnswer: Before the printing press, hand-copied books were extremely costly, since monks had to copy each page by hand, which took months. Gutenberg worked in his workshop, testing his movable metal letters again and again until his press finally worked well. Because of his achievement, many identical copies of a book could be produced quickly, and printed books eventually spread across Europe, changing how people got and shared books forever.

keyWords.definition: to change something completely, often making it much better
keyWords.example: A fresh coat of paint can transform a dull old room.

keyWords.definition: a continent made up of many countries, including places like France, Germany, and Italy
keyWords.example: Her grandparents traveled across Europe by train last summer.

keyWords.definition: a person whose job was to copy documents or books by hand
keyWords.example: The scribe spent years copying a single manuscript by candlelight.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of this article?
options: Hand-copied books were considered perfectly affordable for ordinary families
China's printing methods were identical in every detail to Gutenberg's own design
Gutenberg's mechanism for movable type transformed how books were produced across Europe
Printing presses had no real impact on European society for several centuries
questions.why: The article centers on how Gutenberg's mechanism for movable type transformed book production, solving the costly, slow problem of hand copying.

wrong.A: The article presents hand-copied books as costly, not affordable.
wrong.B: The article notes similarities, not that the methods were identical in every detail.
wrong.D: The article shows printing having an immediate, lasting impact, not a delayed one.

questions.stem: Based on the article, why did hand-copied books fail to meet the needs of most people?
options: They were considered too colorful and visually distracting to read for long hours
They required enormous amounts of time to produce and were therefore extremely costly
They could only legally be owned by trained government officials
They were banned from being read in most European towns
questions.why: The article explains that hand-copied books took enormous amounts of time to produce, making them extremely costly and inaccessible to most people.

wrong.A: Color and visual distraction are never discussed in the article.
wrong.C: Legal ownership restrictions are never mentioned in the article.
wrong.D: No ban on reading books is mentioned anywhere in the article.

questions.stem: What specific combination made Gutenberg's press function so effectively?
options: Metal type, specially prepared ink, and a sturdy mechanism working together
Stone tablets combined with brightly colored paint
Cloth strips woven together with thread
Wooden carvings copied directly from Chinese designs, used one page at a time
questions.why: The article describes Gutenberg's press as combining metal type, specially prepared ink, and a sturdy mechanism to function effectively.

wrong.B: Stone tablets and paint are not described as part of the press.
wrong.C: Cloth and thread are never mentioned as part of the invention.
wrong.D: The article does not say Gutenberg copied designs directly from China.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about innovation from the fact that movable type appeared in China, Korea, and Europe independently?
options: Similar solutions to a shared problem can emerge in separate places
Only European inventors are capable of true innovation
Most inventions in history have had one true creator
Independent inventors rarely succeed without copying others in other lands
questions.why: Movable type developing independently in multiple regions suggests that similar solutions to shared problems can emerge in separate places.

wrong.B: China and Korea developed their own methods, showing innovation was not limited to Europe.
wrong.C: The article shows multiple regions succeeding separately, not one sole creator.
wrong.D: The article describes Gutenberg succeeding without copying anyone directly.

questions.stem: Why does the article emphasize how many exhausting experiments Gutenberg conducted before succeeding?
options: To suggest that persistence through repeated failure can lead to breakthroughs
To show that experimentation ends in complete failure
To prove that Gutenberg's helpers did all of the real work
To argue that testing ideas is generally a waste of valuable time for inventors and printers
questions.why: Highlighting Gutenberg's many exhausting experiments suggests that persistence through failure was essential to his eventual breakthrough.

wrong.B: The article shows experimentation leading to eventual success, not failure.
wrong.C: Gutenberg is credited as leading the effort, working alongside his helpers.
wrong.D: The article presents this testing as essential, not wasteful.

questions.stem: In the article, what does "transform" most precisely describe about Gutenberg's discovery?
options: That it changed book production so completely and fundamentally
That it kept book production exactly the same as before in Europe
That it only affected a single small town in Europe
That it made books slightly more colorful than before
questions.why: The article uses "transform" to show that Gutenberg's discovery changed book production completely, not just slightly.

wrong.B: Transform means to change completely, the opposite of staying the same.
wrong.C: The article describes an effect across the whole of Europe, not one town.
wrong.D: Transform refers to a fundamental change, not simply color.

questions.stem: How does the article's structure support its central idea?
options: It presents the costly problem, the experimentation, and the lasting transformation in sequence
It jumps between unrelated inventions with no clear order, so readers must find the connections
It focuses on describing Gutenberg's personal life story
It only compares the prices of modern printed books
questions.why: The article's sequence, from the costly problem through experimentation to lasting transformation, reinforces its central idea about a historic breakthrough.

wrong.B: The structure follows one invention in a clear, logical order.
wrong.C: Gutenberg's personal life beyond his work is not the article's focus.
wrong.D: Modern book prices are never discussed in the article.

questions.stem: What effect did Gutenberg's mechanism have on the availability of books across Europe?
options: It made books scarcer and even more costly than before in Europe
It allowed many more people to finally obtain and read books
It limited books to use only inside monasteries
It had no measurable effect on book availability
questions.why: Because Gutenberg's mechanism could produce many copies quickly, far more people across Europe could finally obtain and read books.

wrong.A: The article shows books becoming more available and affordable, not scarcer.
wrong.C: The article shows books spreading widely, not staying confined to monasteries.
wrong.D: The article clearly describes books becoming widely available.

HIGH.prompt: Analyze how competition among regions, repeated experimentation, and persistence shaped the development of the printing press, and explain its lasting impact. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: Did you mention movable type developing in more than one region?
Did you explain the role of testing or repeated failure?
Did you connect the invention to its lasting impact on books and ideas?
HIGH.modelAnswer: The printing press developed through independent experimentation across several regions and Gutenberg's own relentless persistence. Movable type had already appeared separately in China and Korea, showing that several places were working toward similar solutions to the same costly problem of hand-copied books. Gutenberg, working in his own workshop with skilled helpers, tested his mechanism of metal type, ink, and a sturdy frame again and again despite repeated failures. His eventual success let identical copies of a book be produced far faster than ever before, transforming how books were made across Europe and eventually the world, so thoroughly that we now read printed books every day without ever considering how remarkable that transformation truly was.

LOW.stem: What problem was Gutenberg trying to solve with his new press?
options: How to make books look more colorful
How to make copying books much faster than by hand
How to make paper cheaper to buy
How to make monks work in bigger buildings
LOW.why: Gutenberg's whole goal was to find a way to make copies of books much faster than the slow process of copying by hand.

wrong.A: Color is never mentioned as Gutenberg's goal.
wrong.C: Paper cost is not the problem the article describes.
wrong.D: Building size for monks is never discussed in the article.

LOW.stem: Why did it matter that many copies of a book could now be made quickly?
options: More people could finally own and read the same book
Books became too easy to lose
Fewer people wanted to read books
Books stopped being written in any language
LOW.why: Because printing made copies quickly, many more people could finally get their own copy of a book to read.

wrong.B: Losing books is not discussed as a result of printing.
wrong.C: The article shows printing leading to more reading, not less.
wrong.D: Books continued being written in many languages, as the article shows.

LOW.stem: What can you tell about Gutenberg from how many tests he tried before succeeding?
options: He gave up quickly when things went wrong
He kept working patiently until his idea succeeded
He did not care whether his press worked
He worked completely alone with no helpers
LOW.why: The article shows Gutenberg trying test after test, which shows he worked patiently and did not give up until his idea worked.

wrong.A: The opposite is true; he kept trying instead of giving up.
wrong.C: He clearly cared a great deal, since he kept testing for a long time.
wrong.D: The article mentions helpers working with him.

LOW.stem: Why does the article end by saying books are everywhere today?
options: To show how much Gutenberg's invention changed how we get books
To say that books are no longer useful
To explain that letters are now written by hand again
To prove that nobody reads books anymore
LOW.why: Ending with books being everywhere today helps readers see how much Gutenberg's invention changed the way we get and read books.

wrong.B: The article shows books are still very useful today.
wrong.C: The article shows printing replaced hand copying, not the reverse.
wrong.D: The article says books are everywhere, meaning people still read them.

MID.stem: What does it suggest that both China, Korea, and Gutenberg independently worked on movable type?
options: Only Gutenberg ever had a good idea about printing
Different inventors in different places can work on similar solutions
Gutenberg secretly copied ideas from Korea
Movable type was invented by accident with no effort
MID.why: The fact that China, Korea, and Gutenberg all developed similar ideas shows that different inventors in different places can work toward similar solutions.

wrong.A: China and Korea also had working ideas before Gutenberg.
wrong.C: The article never claims Gutenberg copied Korea's work.
wrong.D: The article describes careful, deliberate testing, not an accident.

MID.stem: Based on the article, what likely made Gutenberg's press succeed where simple copying could not?
options: It let the same letters be reused to print many pages quickly
It used no letters or ink at all
It required more time than hand copying
It made only one single copy ever
MID.why: Gutenberg's reusable metal letters let him print many pages quickly, something hand copying could never achieve.

wrong.B: The press used metal letters and ink, as the article describes.
wrong.C: The press was faster than hand copying, not slower.
wrong.D: The press could make many copies, not just one.

MID.stem: Why might the article mention how costly hand-copied books were before describing Gutenberg's success?
options: To help readers understand why Gutenberg's achievement mattered so much
To prove that books should always stay expensive
To show that Gutenberg wanted to make books costly too
To explain that monks were paid very well for their work
MID.why: By explaining how costly books once were, the article helps readers understand why Gutenberg's faster, cheaper method was such an important achievement.

wrong.B: The article shows the opposite; Gutenberg made books more affordable.
wrong.C: Gutenberg's goal was to make books cheaper, not costlier.
wrong.D: Monk pay is never discussed in the article.

MID.stem: What is the most likely reason the article ends by describing how many books we can read today?
options: To show how far book production has come since Gutenberg's time
To argue that printed books should be banned
To prove that nobody reads books anymore
To explain exactly how modern printers are built
MID.why: By pointing out how many books we can read today, the article highlights the huge progress made since Gutenberg's invention.

wrong.B: The article presents printing as a positive, lasting achievement.
wrong.C: The article says books are everywhere, meaning people still read them.
wrong.D: Modern printer construction is not explained in the article.

HIGH.stem: What does the article imply about the relationship between repeated failure and historic breakthroughs?
options: Failure has no meaningful connection to eventual breakthroughs
Repeated failure can be a necessary part of reaching a historic breakthrough
A breakthrough always happens on the very first attempt
Scribes should have stopped copying books after one failed try
HIGH.why: Gutenberg's many failed experiments before his eventual success suggest that repeated failure is often necessary on the path to a breakthrough.

wrong.A: The article closely links his many failures to the eventual breakthrough.
wrong.C: The article describes many failed attempts before success, not an immediate one.
wrong.D: Scribes continued their work separately from Gutenberg's testing.

HIGH.stem: Why might historians discuss China, Korea, and Gutenberg together rather than crediting only one inventor?
options: Because independent, separate invention suggests the idea's time had come in multiple places
Because only Gutenberg's press actually produced a single working page
Because Gutenberg and Korean inventors worked in the exact same workshop
Because movable type was invented purely by accident everywhere
HIGH.why: When similar solutions emerge independently in separate regions, it suggests broader historical readiness for the idea rather than one person's sole genius.

wrong.B: Earlier movable type efforts in China and Korea also produced working results.
wrong.C: Gutenberg worked in his own separate European workshop.
wrong.D: The article describes deliberate, careful experimentation, not accident.

HIGH.stem: What underlying assumption does the article make about why wider access to books mattered?
options: That people valued being able to read and own books for themselves
That people had no real interest in reading books at all
That people preferred books to remain rare and expensive
That people were indifferent to how books were produced
HIGH.why: The article's emphasis on books becoming affordable and available implies that people valued the chance to finally read and own books themselves.

wrong.B: The article shows strong demand once books became available.
wrong.C: The article presents affordability as a positive outcome, not a loss.
wrong.D: The article links production methods directly to who could access books.

HIGH.stem: How does the article's closing focus on how easily we read books today serve its larger purpose?
options: It suggests a historic invention can become an unnoticed part of everyday life
It argues that the printing press ultimately failed its original purpose
It proves that nobody values books enough to read them today
It shows that hand-copied books remain the most common format
HIGH.why: By noting how easily we read books today, the article suggests that Gutenberg's historic invention became such an essential, unnoticed part of daily life.

wrong.B: The article presents the press as a celebrated, lasting success.
wrong.C: The article shows books being read constantly, implying high value.
wrong.D: The article explicitly contrasts modern printed books with the slower hand-copied ones of the past.
